Wonderfully
wŭn'dẽr-fu̇l-lĭ
adv. (in a manner to excite wonder or astonishment; marvellously)
Old English wundor, a marvel, with the adverbial ending. The Hebrew pala means to be extraordinary, set apart from the ordinary run of things — the root behind Wonderful as a name of the Messiah in Isaiah 9:6.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The best known use is David's: “I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well” (Psa 139:14). The sentence is the middle term of a psalm about being known — God searching, God besetting behind and before, God seeing the substance yet unperfect — and the wonder is directed at the Maker, not at the thing made. David does not say I am wonderful; he says thou hast made me wonderfully, and the verse before and after both address God directly. The Philistine lords use the word of the plagues: God wrought wonderfully among the Egyptians, and the lesson they draw is that hardening the heart against such works is folly (1Sa 6:6). Daniel uses it of Antichrist's counterfeit: a king of fierce countenance shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper (Dan 8:24) — the same adverb of astonishment turned toward destruction, which is the mark of the counterfeit throughout Scripture, that it astonishes.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wonderfully as in a manner to excite wonder or surprise; marvellously; in a manner surpassing what is usual.

expand to see more

WONDERFULLY, adv. In a manner to excite wonder or surprise.

2. To a wonderful degree; as, wonderfully made.

3. Strangely; in a manner not to be accounted for by ordinary causes.

Key Scripture

Psa 139:14 — "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well."

1Sa 6:6 — "Wherefore then do ye harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? when he had wrought wonderfully among them, did they not let the people go, and they departed?"

Dan 8:24 — "And his power shall be mighty, but not by his own power: and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 139:14 has been reduced to a slogan of self-affirmation, which reverses the psalm: the wonder is directed at the Maker who searches, and the same psalm ends by asking Him to search and try the heart.

expand to see more

The verse is now printed on nursery walls and repeated as a therapeutic assurance about the self, and taken that way it is nearly the opposite of what David wrote. The psalm opens with a God who has searched him and known him, who understands his thought afar off, who compasses his path and his lying down — a knowledge David calls too wonderful for him and from which he cannot flee. Verse 14 stands inside that setting, and its subject is the workmanship, not the workman's pride in himself: marvellous are thy works. Two things go missing when the verse is lifted out. The first is the argument the psalm is actually making, which is against abortion and against the notion that a life in the womb is anything less than the deliberate work of God, since the following verses describe the substance being curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth and all the members written in God's book before there were any of them. The second is the psalm's ending, which is the part slogans never quote: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: and see if there be any wicked way in me. The man who is fearfully and wonderfully made does not conclude that he is fine; he concludes by inviting the searcher in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pala (H6381), to be extraordinary, marvellous, beyond the ordinary; the root of the Messiah's name Pele, Wonderful, in Isaiah 9:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew pala (H6381) — to be surpassing, marvellous, set apart from the ordinary; the verb behind fearfully and wonderfully made; Psalm 139:14.

Hebrew pele (H6382) — a wonder, a marvel; the first of the names given the Child in Isaiah, His name shall be called Wonderful; Isaiah 9:6.

Hebrew alal (H5953) — to deal with, work upon; the Philistine lords' account of what God wrought among the Egyptians; 1 Samuel 6:6.

Usage

"“I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works” — addressed to God, not about the self."

"“When he had wrought wonderfully among them, did they not let the people go?” — the Philistines' argument from the plagues."

"“He shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper” — the counterfeit astonishes too."
